questions.stem: Which enzyme seals the gene into the opened plasmid?

options.explanation: Restriction enzymes cut; they do not seal.
Amylase works on starch.

questions.stem: A gene and a plasmid show matching sticky ends. What follows?

options.text: They anneal and ligase joins them into one unbroken molecule
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Complementary ends attract by base pairing.
Cutting precedes the pairing stage.
The construct stays and functions.

questions.stem: State the two enzyme types used to cut and join DNA.
questions.modelAnswer: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sites and DNA ligase joins the pieces together.

questions.stem: Name the short single-stranded sections formed by cutting DNA.
questions.modelAnswer: Cutting DNA with restriction enzymes leaves sticky ends that pair with complementary overhangs.

questions.stem: Explain why the same restriction enzyme must cut both the gene and the plasmid.
questions.modelAnswer: One enzyme leaves one overhang pattern, so both cut pieces end with complementary sticky ends that can base-pair, allowing ligase to complete the recombinant join.

questions.stem: Designers want a gene inserted at one exact spot in a plasmid. Apply the sequence rule to explain the choice.
questions.modelAnswer: Pick the restriction enzyme whose target sequence occurs once at that spot, so its cut opens the plasmid there and its sticky ends receive the gene precisely.

questions.stem: What is a vector in genetic engineering?

options.text: A protein that reads the code
options.explanation: Reading proteins are not vectors.

options.text: A plasmid or virus that carries DNA into other cells
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Enzymes cut and join; vectors carry.
Sequencing machines are not vectors.

questions.stem: Which cells do viruses transfer DNA into?

options.explanation: Plants are not the taught virus target here.

questions.stem: Which recipients accept DNA from plasmid vectors?

options.explanation: Human cells take viral delivery.

questions.stem: How does a recombinant plasmid spread through a bacterial population?

options.text: The plasmid is copied whenever the bacteria reproduce
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Plasmids migrate between cells like viruses
options.explanation: Copying at division does the spreading.

options.text: The gene mutates into new cells
options.explanation: No mutation is involved.
Natural reproduction handles distribution.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical team needs kilograms of a human protein. Complete the plan with the final stage.

options.explanation: Crops play no role in this route.

options.text: Grow the engineered bacteria in fermenters under controlled conditions
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Inject the plasmids into patients directly
options.explanation: Patients receive purified protein, not plasmids.

questions.stem: State the two structures that act as vectors for recombinant DNA.
questions.modelAnswer: Plasmids and viruses act as vectors, taking up DNA and inserting it into other cells.

questions.stem: Name the term for DNA assembled from separate source pieces.
questions.modelAnswer: DNA combined from different pieces is called recombinant DNA.

questions.stem: Explain why bacteria multiply so usefully for gene product manufacture.
questions.modelAnswer: Bacterial division copies the recombinant plasmid into each descendant, so the population and its gene output grow exponentially in the fermenter.

questions.stem: A therapy must reach human cells, not bacteria. Choose the vector and justify it.
questions.modelAnswer: Choose a viral vector, because viruses transfer DNA into human cells, whereas plasmids serve bacteria or yeast.
